title: Trump Fires NLRB, MSPB, and FTC Members Without Cause
description_short: Trump Fires NLRB, MSPB, and FTC Members Without Cause
description_medium: In late January and early February 2025, Trump fired Gwynne Wilcox from the National Labor Relations Board, Cathy Harris from the Merit Systems Protection Board, and Alvaro Bedoya and Rebecca Kelly Slaughter from the Federal Trade Commission — all without cause, in direct violation of federal statutes that permit removal only for neglect of duty or malfeasance in office.
description_long: In late January and early February 2025, Trump fired Gwynne Wilcox from the National Labor Relations Board, Cathy Harris from the Merit Systems Protection Board, and Alvaro Bedoya and Rebecca Kelly Slaughter from the Federal Trade Commission — all without cause, in direct violation of federal statutes that permit removal only for neglect of duty or malfeasance in office. These multi-member independent agencies were created by Congress with for-cause removal protections upheld by the Supreme Court for 90 years under Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935). Acting Solicitor General Sarah Harris formally informed Congress in February 2025 that the DOJ would no longer defend the constitutional validity of these protections. The Supreme Court, in a 6-3 emergency stay in Trump v. Wilcox (May 2025), allowed the firings to proceed pending full review — with Justice Kagan's dissent warning the majority had allowed Trump to overrule Humphrey's by fiat and signaled the eventual overturn of a foundational check on presidential power.

title: $TRUMP Meme Coin Dinner Sells White House Access to Predominantly Foreign Buyers
description_short: $TRUMP Meme Coin Dinner Sells White House Access to Predominantly Foreign Buyers
description_medium: A competition for a dinner with Trump rewarded major holders of his meme coin, linking token purchases to personal access. Substantial participation by overseas investors and concern from ethics critics. The arrangement raised questions about financial interests and political influence, while participants' nationalities, spending, and later official contacts require careful attribution rather than assumptions about their motives.
description_long: In May 2025, Trump announced that the top 220 holders of his $TRUMP memecoin would receive a private dinner at his Trump National Golf Club in Virginia and the top 25 buyers a White House tour — effectively auctioning presidential access through a personal cryptocurrency. The 220 attendees spent an estimated $148 million combined purchasing coins, all of which flowed to Trump-affiliated entities that hold 80% of the token supply. Researcher Molly White analyzed the winning wallets and determined that 158 of 220 winners (72%) appeared to be foreign nationals based on exchange usage patterns — making their purchases potentially illegal as de facto foreign political contributions. Trump stood at a lectern bearing the presidential seal at the May 22 dinner; Democrats demanded an attendee list but none was released, and ethics experts called it the most brazen pay-for-access scheme in modern presidential history.

title: Trump Vows Day-One Executive Order to End Birthright Citizenship

description_medium: Trump repeatedly promised during the 2024 campaign to issue a first-day executive order ending birthright citizenship for U.S.-born children of undocumented immigrants. description_long: During the 2024 campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly promised to sign an executive order on his first day in office ending birthright citizenship for children born in the United States to undocumented immigrants. He argued that the 14th Amendment had been misinterpreted. The proposal would change the federal government's long-standing recognition of citizenship for nearly everyone born on U.S. soil, regardless of parents' immigration status. The promise drew immediate constitutional questions because the amendment's citizenship clause says people born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens.
